extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry/drama (poets, playwrights, literary critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for composing and judging epic and tragic poetry (plot, diction, metre, use of the marvelous/irrational, and solutions to critical objections), based on Aristotle's Poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-ordinary idiom for distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases which are not part of current idiom give distinction to the style (e.g., δωμάτων ἄπο instead of ἀπὸ δωμάτων).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although such unusual expressions may be ridiculed as unnatural in ordinary speech, their absence from the common idiom is precisely why they lend distinction to poetic style. Example: Ariphrades ridiculed such usages, yet they confer stylistic distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety in modes of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe propriety in the several modes of expression, and in compound words, rare words, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is a great matter to observe what is appropriate for each mode (genre/measure) — misuse can harm the effect. Examples and commentary on appropriate usages are given throughout the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor is singled out as the highest stylistic quality and cannot simply be bestowed; mastery of metaphorical language deeply enhances poetic effect and distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match word-types to genres (compound, rare, metaphorical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of kinds of words: compounds are best adapted to dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, and metaphors to iambic; heroic poetry can make use of all varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose word-types according to genre: compounds → dithyrambs; rare/ornamental words → epic/heroic; metaphors → iambic. In heroic poetry many varieties are serviceable; in iambic (which imitates familiar speech) prefer words also found in prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate diction for iambic verse
rubrics_metrics.description: In iambic verse, the most appropriate words are those which are found even in prose: the current or proper, the metaphorical, the ornamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because iambic verse aims to reproduce familiar speech, avoid excessively rare or alien diction there; select words that preserve a sense of the ordinary while allowing metaphor and ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot (single action) for narrative imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot ought, as in a tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles: it should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A unified plot resembles a living organism and produces the pleasure proper to it. Avoid composing the poem as a mere sequence of loosely connected events that do not converge to a single result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-vast subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to make a poem of an excessively vast subject (e.g., the whole war of Troy); detach a single portion instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a theme is too large it becomes over-complicated or unwieldy; select a manageable portion or single hero/period/action to maintain unity and intelligibility (Homer's method: detach a portion, admit episodes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes in epic to diversify and add mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry can admit many events and episodes relevant to the subject; these increase the poem's bulk and contribute to grandeur and variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes (e.g., Catalogue of ships) can diversify the poem and relieve sameness, but they should be relevant to the subject and not produce incoherence or satiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts required in epic (reversal, recognition, scenes of suffering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic must have the same kinds of parts as tragedy (except song and spectacle): reversals, recognitions, and scenes of suffering; thoughts and diction must be artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if scale and metre differ, the structural elements that produce dramatic pleasure remain essential in epic composition; follow these technical requirements to achieve artistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and metre suitability (heroic metre for epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic differs from tragedy chiefly in its scale and in its metre; the heroic measure is the stateliest and most massive and therefore most fitting for epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The heroic metre admits rare words and metaphors and suits a large narrative. Composing large-scale narrative in other metres or mixing metres (as Chaeremon did) is incongruous and absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing metres
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing different metres in a large-scale narrative is inappropriate and appears incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For dignity and coherence, maintain a single appropriate metre (heroic for epics); mixing (trochaic, iambic, heroic together) undermines the unity and tone of the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's self-effacement
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; he is an imitator and should at once bring in characters with distinct personal traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-use of authorial intrusions diminishes imitation. Homer is praised for introducing characters quickly and letting their characteristic qualities appear through action and speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the wonderful and the irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is required in Tragedy; the irrational (on which the wonderful depends) has wider scope in Epic because the actor is not seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The marvelous pleases; the irrational can be tolerated more readily in epic narrative (where it is reported) than on stage (where it may look ludicrous). Use the wonder/irrational where it fits genre and does not break believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities; the tragic plot must not be composed of irrational parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing incidents, select those that are more credible within poetic probability (even if strictly impossible) rather than unlikely-but-possible events that strain the audience's acceptance. Irrational elements should, if possible, lie outside the action of the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: If introducing the irrational, make it plausible
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an irrational element is introduced and an air of likelihood imparted to it, we must accept it in spite of absurdity; the poet can veil the absurd by poetic charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The audience will infer earlier events from later truths (the fallacy exploited). Use craft to make improbable elements felt as acceptable—e.g., Homer’s skill in presenting apparently absurd incidents convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction elaborated in pauses of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action where there is no expression of character or thought; over-brilliant diction in speaking parts obscures character and thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate or highly polished language for descriptive or non-dramatic passages; when character and thought must be clear, avoid diction that distracts or conceals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types of poetic faults (essential vs accidental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within poetry there are two kinds of faults: those that touch its essence (inherent inability to imitate) and those accidental (wrong choice or technical errors in other arts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An error of capacity (imitating incorrectly) is more serious than an incidental technical mistake (e.g., ignorance of veterinary detail). When assessing faults, consider whether they undermine the poetic art's essential ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors may be justified by artistic ends
rubrics_metrics.description: An error may be justified if, by violating a special rule of the art, the end of the art (the intended effect) is better attained; but if the end could be attained without violating rules, the error is not justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate deviations from technical correctness by whether they produce a superior artistic effect. Avoid errors unless necessary to achieve the poem's proper end; prefer solutions that preserve art's rules when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and answer critical objections (five sources, twelve solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical objections are drawn from five sources (e.g., impossibility, irrationality, harmfulness, opposition, violation of artistic correctness), and solutions may be sought under twelve heads previously enumerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding to critics, identify whether the charge is that something is impossible, irrational, harmful, contrary to artistic correctness, etc., and apply one of the prescribed types of solutions (e.g., show probability, justification by artistic purpose, linguistic usage, punctuation/intonation, ambiguity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of representational object (three kinds to imitate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must imitate one of three objects: things as they were or are, things as they are said or thought to be, or things as they ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the mode of representation (realistic, conventional, or idealized) early; the chosen mode will govern acceptable liberties and how to justify departures from everyday reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve interpretive difficulties by language features
rubrics_metrics.description: Many textual or interpretive difficulties are solvable by reference to accent/breathing, punctuation, ambiguity of words, dialectal or customary usages, or the intended metaphorical sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ambiguous verbs resolved by punctuation; rare words understood by dialectal usage (e.g., οὐρῆας meaning sentinels); metaphorical uses of ‘all’ meaning ‘many’. Use philological and contextual tools to defend or clarify passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrational incidents within the dramatic action
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational incidents (that do not fit the internal logic of the drama) should, if possible, be excluded or placed outside the action (e.g., not reported within the play itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of problematic placements include a hero’s ignorance of a crucial fact taking place within the drama or an implausible messenger’s report; construct the plot so that essential improbabilities do not arise from faulty plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret linguistic oddities by usage and multiple senses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a word seems inconsistent, consider how many senses it may bear in context; choose the reading that best fits the circumstances (e.g., 'spear was stayed' can mean several things).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not hastily condemn apparent inconsistencies; examine dialectal meanings, metaphorical extension, and plausible readings consistent with the speaker, audience, and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a single hero, period, or single action with multiplicity of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: For coherent narrative effect, choose a single hero or single period or a single action (which may have many parts) rather than attempting to cover too many protagonists or stretches of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic and tragic coherence improves when focus is narrowed to a central subject, even while allowing episodic material that relates back to the core action.
